newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: UNHCR freezes Kabul programmes citing security.
newsitem.headline: UNHCR freezes Kabul programmes citing security.

text.p: The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said on Wednesday that it was putting most of its activities in Kabul on hold because of arrests and intimidation of its staff by the ruling Taleban militia.
""We are putting on hold most of our programmes in Kabul until the security situation improves," Rupert Colville, a spokesman for the UNHCR, said.

He said that four of the 22 local staff in the UNHCR's main office in Kabul had been arrested, while seven Afghan women employees had been told to stay at home since the Islamic Taleban movement captured Kabul on September 27.
"We are extremely concerned about the safety of our four arrested staffers, one of whom has been missing for nearly four weeks," Colville said. "The rest of the staff are petrified."
The virtual suspension of UNHCR activities coincides with the start of a vital winter relief programme for Kabul.
The agency says that effective security guarantees are lacking, despite assurances given by the Taleban authorities.
Colville said a UNHCR driver was arrested while shopping at a pharmacy in Kabul on October 26 and had not been released. Despite strenuous efforts, his whereabouts were unknown.
Armed men entered the agency's Kabul office on November 5, thereby violating a 1946 U.N. Convention safeguarding the privileges and immunities of United Nations agencies.
Gunmen entered the UNHCR office again on November 12 and abducted a driver, a logistical assistant and a messenger.

Late the same day 16 armed men forcibly entered the home of Terry Pitzner, an American who heads the UNHCR office in Kabul, and spent five hours looking for, and questioning him about, a local Afghan staff member, Colville said.
Other international relief agencies and news organisations operating in Kabul say their local staff have also faced increasing harassment by the Taleban in recent weeks.

The Taleban's acting Foreign Minister, Mullah Mohammad Ghous, said in a recent letter to U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali that the movement wanted to cooperate with U.N. peace efforts, but felt that it was being unfairly treated.

"We deeply regret that forces inimical to the unity and peace in Afghanistan have continued to present a completely distorted picture of our policies and approach to redressing the socio-economic problems of Afghanistan," he wrote.

"It is necessary for the international community to take an objective view of the Afghan society and give due credence to the fact that areas under the control of the interim (Taleban) government are peaceful, with fundamental rights of the people fully protected," Ghous said in his letter.
